sentences.text: The skull of Telmatosaurus measured roughly 40 centimeters in length, featuring a narrow shape that stood quite high at the rear.
Its teeth were tall and slender, with a width of approximately four millimeters.
This dinosaur reached a length of about 5 meters and a mass of 600 kilograms, a size attributed to insular dwarfism.
A juvenile Telmatosaurus examined by Dumbrava et al. possesses a large, non-cancerous growth known as an ameloblastoma, a condition previously found only in modern mammals and reptiles.
Peasants discovered a Telmatosaurus skull in 1895 at the Săcele estate in Transylvania and gave it to Ilona Nopcsa.
Franz Nopcsa originally named the species Limnosaurus transsylvanicus in 1899.
Nopcsa renamed the genus Telmatosaurus in 1903 after finding that Limnosaurus was already used for a crocodilian described in 1872.
The generic name derives from the Greek word for 'swamp', reflecting the belief that the animal had aquatic habits.
In 1910, Barnum Brown named the genus Hecatasaurus, unaware of the name change, creating a later synonym.
Nopcsa transferred the species to the genus Orthomerus in 1915, naming it Orthomerus transsylvanicus.
The name Telmatosaurus was revived in the 1980s because the genus Orthomerus was considered a nomen dubium.
The presence of an ameloblastoma in a dinosaur suggests that benign tumor development is a basal characteristic.
Because only the lower jaws are preserved, the cause of death for the juvenile Telmatosaurus with the tumor cannot be determined.
Magyar and colleagues named the clade containing Telmatosaurus, Kryptohadros, and Tethyshadros as Telmatosauridae.
The family classification of Telmatosaurus is listed as Hadrosauridae with uncertainty, though it is also considered a member of the clade Telmatosauridae.
Current cladistic analyses suggest Telmatosaurus is either a basal member of Hadrosauridae or occupies a basal position in the broader Hadrosauroidea.
Telmatosaurus belongs to the class Ornithischia.
In 1900, Nopcsa assigned Telmatosaurus to Trachodontidae, a term that is no longer used.
Telmatosaurus transsylvanicus lived between 70 and 66 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous in what is now Europe.
At that time, the land where the fossils were found was part of the European archipelago.
It is debated whether fragmentary hadrosauroid material from Spain, France, Germany, and Romania belongs to Telmatosaurus, as an identity is difficult to prove.
It is debated whether fragmentary material from Spain, France, and Germany, previously included in Orthomerus, truly belongs to Telmatosaurus, as it is difficult to prove the identity.
Some material was lost during World War II due to bombings, complicating the study of the species.
